points: The Union Labour Ministry has constituted the National Social Security Boards for Unorganised Workers and Gig and Platform Workers under the Code on Social Security.
These Boards aim to strengthen social protection for vulnerable workers through welfare schemes, institutional oversight, and recommended measures.
The central concern is that their centralised composition and representation gaps raise issues about inclusive decision-making and cooperative federalism.
The Board for Unorganised Sector Workers has 40 nominated members, including 7 representatives each from workers and employers, chaired by the Union Labour Minister.
The Board for Gig and Platform Workers has 22 members, including 5 representatives each from aggregators and workers, alongside 5 State Government representatives.
Both Boards primarily perform advisory and monitoring functions, while scheme notification and implementation rely on the competent government and designated agencies.
Financing frameworks can involve contributions from the Centre, States, aggregators, workers, or CSR funds, with aggregator contributions set at 1% to 2% of annual turnover.
Challenges include centralised governance, federal friction due to labour being in the Concurrent List, representation gaps, and portability difficulties for migrant workers.
Success requires inclusive representation, sustainable financing, institutional reforms, Centre-State coordination, and portable welfare entitlements.
sum.text:
The Union Labour Ministry has constituted the National Social Security Boards for Unorganised Workers and Gig and Platform Workers under the Code on Social Security. These Boards aim to strengthen social protection for vulnerable workers through welfare schemes and institutional oversight. However, their centralised composition and representation gaps raise concerns about inclusive decision-making and cooperative federalism. Effective implementation, adequate financing and stakeholder participation are essential to achieve meaningful social security.
Meaning: Social security protects individuals against economic and social distress arising from old age, unemployment, sickness, disability, work injury, maternity and loss of the breadwinner .
Constitutional Basis: Entries 23 and 24 of the Concurrent List cover social security, social insurance, employment and welfare-related matters, enabling both the Centre and States to legislate in relevant areas.
Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP): Article 41 provides for public assistance in cases of unemployment, old age, sickness and disability, subject to the State’s economic capacity. Article 42 promotes humane working conditions and maternity relief, while Article 43 calls for a living wage and decent standard of life.
Workforce Size: The NITI Aayog’s June 2022 report estimated 77 lakh gig workers in 2020–21 , projecting an increase to 2.35 crore by 2029–30 . These figures are estimates and projections.
Employment Share: Gig workers constituted 2.6% of the non-agricultural workforce in 2020–21, projected to rise to 6.7% by 2029–30 . Their corresponding shares of the total workforce were estimated at 1.5% and 4.1% , respectively.
Welfare Measures: The Union Budget 2025–26 announced identity cards, e-Shram registration and healthcare coverage under Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (PM-JAY) for gig workers, with nearly 1 crore workers expected to benefit.
Registration: The e-Shram portal had registered 31.82 crore unorganised workers as of 3 August 2026, including workers from different categories. Registration does not necessarily establish actual receipt of social security benefits .
Legal Basis: Section 6 of the Code on Social Security provides for the constitution of the National Social Security Board for Unorganised Workers , chaired by the Union Minister for Labour and Employment. The separate Board for Gig and Platform Workers is constituted under the relevant provisions of the Code.

<p>The <a href="https://www.deccanherald.com/tags/mangaluru">Mangaluru City Corporation’</a>s decision to impose fines of Rs 1,000 to Rs 5,000 on pet owners who fail to clean up their dogs’ excreta in public places is a welcome move. Their success, however, will depend more on enforcement than the severity of the penalties.
Pet waste is a frequent source of friction in apartment complexes, parks, and residential neighbourhoods. While keeping pets is a legitimate personal choice, allowing them to foul public spaces without cleaning up reflects a disregard for civic responsibility. Too often, public areas are treated as extensions of private premises, with little concern for the inconvenience caused to others.
At the same time, pet owners’ rights cannot be curtailed through arbitrary restrictions imposed by residents’ associations or housing societies.</p>.<p>The <a href="https://www.deccanherald.com/tags/karnataka-high-court">Karnataka High Court</a> addressed this tension in November 2024, directing the erstwhile Bruhat Bengaluru Mahanagara Palike (BBMP) to amend its bye-laws to impose higher penalties against owners who fail to clean up after their pets. Importantly, it reaffirmed that the liberty of pet owners to walk their dogs in public spaces must coexist with the equally important right of other citizens to a clean environment. Mere assurances of compliance, the court observed, are not enough.
Comprehensive guidelines issued by the BBMP the same year also require owners to carry biodegradable waste bags and clean up immediately after their pets. They also lay down norms on leashing, vaccination, registration, identification tags, and the rights of pets in residential complexes. However, compliance remains patchy.</p>.Bengaluru reworks on pet dogs policy, canines above 3 months may have to be registered under new laws.<p class="bodytext">The government has repeatedly sought to define the responsibilities of pet owners, apartment associations, and those who feed community dogs.

The issue is not about denying people the joy of celebrating Diwali. As the SC rightly observed, it is a festival of lights, not gunpowder. NEW DELHI: The population enumeration phase of Census 2027 will last longer than in past census exercises, with its duration spanning nearly one-and-a-half months from Jan 10 to Feb 28, including the 15-day self-enumeration window, as against the earlier Phase-2 duration of 20 days, conventionally running from Feb 9-28. Sources told TOI that the house-to-house population enumeration schedule announced earlier for poll-bound states of Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Goa and Punjab also spans 35 days. The longer duration may be linked to the increased number of questions at 40, including pertaining to caste, to be asked in Phase-2 of Census 2027, as against 29 in 2011.
No census has been declared in Manipur. The census exercise in the state was put on hold after demands from various sections within the state that the National Register of Citizens (NRC) exercise be conducted first. A notification issued by the Union home ministry Friday declared that a nationwide census of population shall be undertaken - except in Manipur (till further declaration); poll-bound states of Goa, UP, Punjab and Uttarakhand, where it was preponed in view of the impending assembly elections early next year; and UT of Ladakh and snow-bound, non-synchronous areas of Himachal Pradesh and UT of Jammu & Kashmir, where it has already been completed - from Jan 25 to Feb 27, 2027.
This shall be preceded by a window of self-enumeration from Jan 10-24. While the reference date for Census 2027 has already been declared as March 1, 2027, a revisional round will be conducted from March 1-5, 2027. The new fields to be captured in Phase-2 of Census include, apart from caste, spouse's name and mother and father's particulars, the respondent's nationality as declared, permanent address, place of Covid-19 vaccination, total number of bank accounts, mobile number, Aadhaar number, voter ID number, passport number and availability of driving licence.
